content: The World Health Organization (WHO) advises against the use of lateral flow urine lipoarabinomannan assay (LF-LAM) for diagnosing active tuberculosis (TB) in the following scenarios: 1. HIV-positive adults, adolescents, and children without first evaluating TB symptoms. 2. HIV-positive individuals who do not exhibit TB symptoms and have either an unknown CD4 cell count or a CD4 cell count of 100 cells/mm³ or higher. 3. HIV-negative individuals. In lowand middle-income countries, WHO recommends the use of interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) to detect latent TB infection. However, these tests should not be used to diagnose pulmonary or extrapulmonary TB, nor should they be employed in the diagnostic evaluation of adults, including those who are HIV-positive, suspected of having active TB. The treatment of TB has undergone significant advancements in recent years, with the introduction of new drugs and regimens. Consequently, the definitions for drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) have been updated. The revised definition of pre-extensively drug-resistant TB (pre-XDR-TB) is TB caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains that meet the criteria for multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB) and are also resistant to any fluoroquinolone (FQ). The updated definition of extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) includes resistance to bedaquiline (BDQ) or linezolid (LZD) in addition to MDR/RR-TB and FQ resistance. These changes have significant implications for member states, particularly in scaling up the detection of resistance to FQs and BDQ. There is also an increasing demand for drug susceptibility testing (DST) for other new and repurposed drugs. In 2018, WHO updated the critical concentrations (CCs) used in phenotypic DST to include these new and repurposed drugs. A WHO technical manual for DST is available to guide laboratories in implementing these changes. The new definition of XDR-TB requires DST results for FQs, BDQ, and LZD, making testing for resistance to BDQ and LZD a priority, especially for BDQ resistance. Phenotypic DST for BDQ and LZD can be performed using either the mycobacterial growth indicator tube (MGIT) or Middlebrook 7H11 media. The BDQ pure drug substance for phenotypic DST is provided free of charge through the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) HIV Reagent Program, although courier costs must be covered. Revisions to DST protocols are expected to reduce discrepancies between genotypic and phenotypic DST results. Laboratories are advised to implement these changes immediately. For MGIT, this can be achieved by reconstituting the lyophilized rifampicin (RIF) from the BD SIRE kit in 8 mL of sterile distilled or deionized water instead of 4 mL. Phenotypic DST remains the reference standard for most anti-TB drugs, but it is slow and requires specialized infrastructure and highly skilled staff. New and rapid next-generation technologies are needed at the peripheral level to expedite appropriate therapy and improve patient outcomes. DNA sequencing using next-generation sequencing (NGS) is a promising method for rapidly detecting mutations associated with drug resistance for many anti-TB drugs. NGS-based DST could reduce the reliance on phenotypic DST for patient care decisions and drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) surveys. It may be particularly useful for drugs where phenotypic DST is unreliable or in settings lacking the capacity to perform phenotypic DST. Current NGS systems have limitations, including the need for computational expertise and resources. Amplification-based targeted NGS assays for detecting DR-TB directly from sputum specimens have been developed. For example, the Deeplex-MycTB assay, commercially available in CE-IVD and RUO versions, can predict resistance to 15 anti-TB drugs with a turnaround time of less than 48 hours. However, these assays have not yet been reviewed or approved by WHO for clinical use. One major challenge with these technologies is the lack of a standardized and robust single reference source for interpreting mutations. To address this, WHO has developed guidance and released a catalog of mutations in the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) and their association with drug resistance. This catalog is the largest database of MTBC isolates with matched phenotypic DST and whole genome sequences, and regular updates are planned. It is also expected to support the development of other rapid molecular DST methods. Diagnostic tests implemented within TB laboratory networks should provide accurate and timely results to impact clinical decision-making, be justified based on need, and be quality-assured, reliable, and reproducible. The placement of diagnostic tests within the laboratory network is critical to achieving these outcomes. In resource-limited or high-burden settings, TB laboratory networks often have a pyramidal structure, with the largest number of laboratories at the peripheral level (Level I), a moderate number at the intermediate level (Level II), and a single or few central laboratories (Level III) at the provincial, state, or national level. At the peripheral level, laboratories focus on basic diagnostic tests for initial TB detection, such as LF-LAM, acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear microscopy, and nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) like Xpert MTB/RIF and Truenat MTB. These tests are suitable for use in clinics and care centers for people living with HIV (PLHIV) and other populations. However, LF-LAM lacks drug-resistance detection and should be used as a complementary test. At the intermediate level, laboratories offer more sophisticated technologies requiring advanced infrastructure, expertise, or biosafety precautions. Reliable and rapid sample transport networks are essential for connecting peripheral and intermediate laboratories. Moderate complexity automated NAATs and culture-based methods may be applicable at this level, but these are gradually being replaced by more automated and rapid alternatives. At the central level, laboratories provide highly advanced testing, including resolving discordant results, troubleshooting, training, quality assurance, and surveillance. Technologies such as NGS, first-line and second-line line-probe assays (FL-LPA and SL-LPA), and high-complexity reverse hybridization NAATs are suitable for this level. Phenotypic DST for new and repurposed drugs should also be available. The structure of the TB diagnostic network and the testing packages available at each level should be tailored to meet the needs of the community and the local TB epidemiology. Careful logistical planning, including mapping the current network of health facilities, population densities, testing burden, transport infrastructure, and available laboratory resources, will aid in the effective placement of diagnostic tests.
